issues.text: False about the code. Line 23 at stage-0 is 'Assert.Equal(new[] { 0, 60_000, 0 }, kinds.Select(kind => kind.ForOrder(2_000_000)));' - it contains no 'ShippingFee' token (git grep at stage-0 lists only lines 7, 10, 12, 21). The type is named on line 21 ('new ShippingFee[]'), and the lambda parameter on line 23 is literally 'kind', so a reader who opens the line sees the opposite of 'names only ShippingFee, never a kind'.
issues.fix: Replace the sentence with: "Line 23 calls `ForOrder` on each element of the `ShippingFee[]` array from line 21 and never names `StandardShipping`, `ExpressShipping` or `PickUpInStore`; each object brought its own fee rule with it."
issues.quote: Line 23 names only `ShippingFee`, never a kind; each object brought its own fee rule with it.

issues.text: Referent of 'it' is the abstract method, so the sentence says classes derive from a method. Classes derive from the class that declares it (inheritance.md:41 'must be overridden in any non-abstract class that directly inherits from that class'). Section 3 has the same ambiguity: 'a method the base type declares ... every class that derives directly from it'.
issues.fix: Section 4: "because an abstract method must get a body in every non-abstract class that derives directly from the class declaring it." Section 3: "every class that derives directly from the base type and is not itself abstract must supply the body, marked `override`."
issues.quote: because an abstract method must get a body in every class that derives directly from it and is not abstract

issues.text: 'only such a class may declare an abstract method' is true among classes but not absolute: abstract.md:63 'You can declare static abstract and static virtual methods in interfaces.' Scratch build (SDK 10.0.300) of an interface declaring 'abstract int Instance();' and 'static abstract int Static();' compiles with no diagnostic. The next lesson sets interfaces beside abstract classes, so the absolute wording will be contradicted.
issues.fix: Replace the clause with the rule for classes: "...cannot be created with `new`, and a class that declares an abstract method must itself be marked `abstract`." (inheritance.md:45 'if a class does contain an abstract member, the class itself must be declared as abstract').
issues.quote: and only such a class may declare an abstract method

issues.text: The bold definition makes polymorphism a call to an abstract method through a base-type variable, where section 3 defines base type as a class. Section 6 then says a call through the other kind of type (not a class) also runs the actual class's method, i.e. is polymorphism too, so the lesson contradicts its own definition. Docs tie it to virtual members generally (inheritance.md:41 'Abstract and virtual members are the basis for polymorphism').
issues.fix: Keep the sentence and scope it: "...so different objects answer the same call differently. This lesson shows it with an abstract method on a base type; section 6 names another way." Claim 21 needs no change.
issues.quote: a call to an abstract method, written once through a variable declared as the base type, runs the override in the object's actual type

issues.text: True only because the kind is a string (section 2); section 4 drops that condition. Scratch build, SDK 10.0.300: a switch expression over an enum with no discard arm gives 'warning CS8509 ... the pattern 'Probe.Kind.Fourth' is not covered' - the compiler does name the missing kind. Stated bare, a reader will carry it to enums.
issues.fix: "...each new kind must be added to every one, and because the kind is a string, the compiler does not notice a miss." (claim 6 already carries the string condition).
issues.quote: each new kind must be added to every one, and the compiler does not notice a miss

'directly' and 'not itself abstract' also hint at cases the lesson never shows (a class two steps below ShippingFee, an abstract class deriving from it). I re-read both sentences twice.
issues.fix: In section 3, section 4 and the q4 explanation, write 'derives directly from the base type' instead of 'from it', and give in section 3 a one-clause example of what 'directly' leaves out.

issues.text: I read this misconception twice. The 'you notice this' part packs a need (a shared invoice-line call), two classes that exist nowhere in the lesson (a payment class, an invoice-line class) and the one-class-after-':' rule into two long sentences. I got why deriving fails, but only on the second pass.
